chapter: Singers, Las Vegas, Hodges and road life
title: Standing up to Beldon Katleman at the El Rancho Vegas
summary: Barnet's quintet refused to change its hours; he threatened a parking lot gig, then invoked a Petrillo scale of 1,500 dollars.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: I read several accounts of your differences with [Beldon Cattleman] in Las Vegas, and I love the story. Tell it for me, will you?

Well, we were booked in there. This was a quintet. I had Buddy Childers and Ralph Pena Pinaud, Art Anton and Bob Harrington, and we were supposed to play in the lounge, you know. So the contract says 11:00 to 4:00, and we go up there, we play there a few days, and Beldon comes over to me and says, "We're changing the hours. You're going to play from 12:00 to 6:00." I said, "No, we're not going to change any hours." I said, "You're a businessman and I'm sure you read the contract before you signed it. I did." I said, "We're going to play 11:00 till 4:00." And he said no. I said oh, yeah. So the first thing he started, we'd go to work at 11:00 o'clock, and he turned off all the lights in the room and the mike, and we're playing up there all by ourselves, and we'd play, "Dancing in the Dark," and we'd start out in C and everybody would take a whole bunch of choruses on that, and then we'd go to D-flat and everybody'd -- the same tune --
and we'd play choruses on that, and we went the whole scale, you know. And then at 12:00 o'clock we'd turn the lights on. But then we'd quit at 4:00.
What did you play then, 'I'm Beginning to See the Light?'
No, we didn't play anything.
I mean at 12:00 o'clock.

Oh, no, he'd turn the lights on and then we'd just go ahead and do our thing, and he'd get up to dance, because they were able to dance there at the -- and every time he'd get up on the floor to dance I'd play, 'Cottontail,' at a breakneck tempo, you know, and --
(Laughter)

So finally he said, 'Well, tomorrow night you guys are going to play in the parking lot.' And I said, 'The parking lot?' So I called up Petrillo and I explained to him what was going on, and he sent him a wire. He said, 'Special scale for bands playing in the parking lot. Side man, $1,500.00 a week. Leader, $5,000.' Well, that was the end of that.
(Laughter)
So I finally compromised with him and I said, 'We'll give you one more hour, we'll play from 11:00 to 5:00, but I'm not going to 6:00.' So we finished the thing out.
That was what year?
Oh, I think that was around '53.
Was it El Rancho Vegas, was that the --
The Rancho, yeah, the El Rancho.
I like that.

Well, you know, a lot of guys said to me, "Aren't you worried about them guys up in Vegas?" I said I wasn't worried a bit, because all them guys, as you called them, hated Beldon. And they were secretly slapping their thighs and having a wonderful time about the whole thing. In fact I had a couple of them said, "Hang in there, kid. It's great. It's funny."
(Laughter)
I think it's the only case I ever heard of anybody standing up to anybody in Las Vegas, I mean management.
Well, I tell you, if it had been elsewhere I wouldn't have done it, but -- I'd probably be walking with a limp now --
If you were walking.
Yeah.
